  loop the solver never reached (inside an opaque `catch` body), a guarded
  body, and a stub-declared loop command the CFG keeps as a call draw what
  they drew before. The per-item path carries the queue as it carries
  every other walk-recorded one: `BodyFragment` holds a body's candidates,
  `rebase_fragment_pending` shifts their spans and
  `graft_fragment_pending` extends the shell's queue, without which a loop
  inside a proc body was resolved by no unit and reported nothing on the
  incremental path. Deltas: `set n 0; while {$n} {puts x}` reports W240
  where W242 was (the counter `n` is never modified, which the text said);
  `set go 1; while {$go} {puts x}` reports W241 where W242 was;
  `for {set i 0} {$i < 10} {} {puts hi}` reports W241 where W242 was; and
  `for {set i 0} {$i < 0} {incr i} {puts hi}` reports W240 where nothing
  was, the step modifying the counter.

- **D187 — the iRules flow checks read applied reachability, by
  statement where they walk the IR** (VT6.6). Two walks read the structured
  IR body of a `::when::` procedure, not the CFG's blocks — IRULE1201 and
  IRULE1202 (`find_http_flow_warnings`) and IRULE5002 and IRULE5004
  (`find_unguarded_drop_warnings`) — so neither can skip a block. Each
  takes the unit's `unreached_statements`: the spans of the statements only
  blocks the solver proved unreachable hold (a statement any executable
  block holds is reached, and one the graph does not hold at all — a body
  it keeps as one call — is not listed), and a step over such a statement
  leaves the path states as they were (`FlowDispatch::unreached`). The
  branch shapes are untouched: an `if` keeps its condition-false path and a
  loop its zero-iteration path, so a walk states the same paths minus the
  effects of statements that never run. A path is not pruned where the
  solver decided the branch — `if {1} {event disable all}` after a `drop`
  still leaves a condition-false path with the drop unguarded — which is a
  precision these walks never had and no item asked for. The walks over the
  CFG's blocks read `executable_blocks` as the IRULE3102 and collect walks
  already do: IRULE4002 skips a block the solver proves unreachable, and
  IRULE4004's write counts, which take every write of every event so that a
  second write anywhere disqualifies the first, count only the blocks a
  solved event proves reachable, a complexity-guarded event — with no
  solver run to prove anything — still counting all of its blocks. A
  `clientside`, `serverside` or `peer` body is a script the collect-flow
  scan lowers on its own (`scan_side_switch_body`); it now builds a
  `FunctionUnit` over that lowering and skips the blocks the unit proves
  unreachable, so IRULE1005 to IRULE1008 read the reachability inside the
  body as they read it in the event around it. Deltas: `if {0} {HTTP::respond
  200}; HTTP::header insert X-Custom val` reports no IRULE1201, nor does the
  `set flag 0` form, a `while {0}` body, a dead `switch` arm, or a header
  command after an `if {1} {return}`; a second `HTTP::respond` in a dead arm
  reports no IRULE1202; a `drop` or `DNS::return` in a dead arm no IRULE5002
  or IRULE5004; a `set static::debug` in a dead arm no IRULE4002, the
  warning landing on the write that runs; a `TCP::collect` in a dead arm of a
  `clientside` body no IRULE1007. IRULE4004 reports one finding more where
  the only other write of a variable sits in an arm the solver proves dead
  (`set svc foo; if {0} {set svc bar}`), because that write never runs; the
  migration page's "fewer findings in dead arms" does not say so, and the
  write counts are among the walks the item names.

Taken while slice 9 was executed (§ *Slice 9* › *Record (2026-09-30):
slice 9* has the witnesses):

- **D188 — Nested writes ride on the outcome as resolved places** (VT9.1).
  The page says the state's writes become the invocation's ordered stores,
  but a `StoreOutcome` names its place by a `TargetId`, an operand of the
  invocation that ran it, and the write of a nested `[incr x]` names an
  operand of `incr`, not of the `expr` around it: a consumer that resolved
  it through the outer inputs would read another word. So
  `InvocationOutcome` gains `nested_writes: Vec<(PlaceRef, StoreOutcome)>` —
  the pairs `EvaluationState::writes` already holds — applied ahead of
  `ordered_stores`; `has_stores` counts them, and an error completion's
  `written` counts across them and then the ordered stores, which
  `validate_outcome` checks. The stores' types are not carried: a definition
  a nested write makes states no folded type.
- **D189 — The read rule is the registry's, and `variable` keeps its
  program-point meaning** (VT9.1). `AnalysisInputs::variable` has no state
  parameter, so "`variable` consults `writes` first" is
  `EvaluationState::written` / `written_in` (`inputs.rs`), one function with
  two readers: `ExprServices::var`, state first and then the inputs, and the
  lattice inputs' overlay (`LatticeInputs::prior_writes`, read by
  `named_fact`, `prior_store` and the existence reads), which is how a nested
  command sees the writes made before it. The last write naming a place
  decides; a preserve changes nothing; a write that only shares storage with
  it (an element beside its array), a may-write and an unbind leave it
  unknown, which declines.
- **D190 — What `LocalWrites` admits** (VT9.1). A nested outcome's writes are
  applied when every one is a preserve, of any place, or a `Write` or
  `WriteElement` to a place the state owns (`LatticeDriver::state_owns`: not
  traced, not escaping, and not an element of an array that is); an error
  completion applies the first `written` of them. A may-write, an unbind, a
  completion code that is not an error, a store to a place no resolver can
  name (a computed name, an element beside its array) and a traced or
  escaping place are `StatefulNested` — placement failures map to it rather
  than keep their own reason, as the page's "any other outcome" reads. The
  policy admits every outcome `EffectFreeOnly` does, a preserve being
  admitted whatever it names. An existence query declines once the
  evaluation has touched its place (`[info exists x]` after `[set x 1]` is
  `StatefulNested`), and the enclosing writes' existence reads answer
  `Bound(Scalar)` for a write. The members of a finite input must agree on
  result, completion and writes, or the answer is `CorrelatedSets`, as
  before.
- **D191 — An ended evaluation is an answer, not a decline** (VT9.1). A
  nested outcome that did not complete normally ends the evaluation at that
  command (`ExprStop::Ended`, `ExprAnswer::Ended`), and `ExpressionEvaluation`
  turns an error into an outcome whose completion is `Error { written }`,
  with the state's writes and no exact result. No route in the tree yields an
  error completion (`error` has no semantics; VT10.1 makes a core's
  `CmdError` one), so the path is pinned with a scripted nested service, and
  the driver still publishes nothing for it: `apply_outcome` declines any
  non-normal completion (D107) until slice 10 publishes per path.
- **D192 — The host of an embedded call is found by adjacency and span**
  (VT9.2). The plan has the synthetic
  call carry its host's index. The builder emits the call immediately before
  its host and gives both the host's span, which is what D169 already
  identifies them by, and an index recorded at build time is stale the moment
  anything is inserted between them, so the solver reads the pair off the
  block instead: a call with the marker, followed by a statement that is not a
  call of that kind and has the same span. `SyntheticMarker` and the IR stay
  as they are.

Taken in the review of slice 6 (§ *Slice 6* › *Record (2026-09-30): review
fixes for slice 6* has the witnesses):

- **D193 — An opaque `switch` defines every name its arms may write**
  (review fix 1, B1). A `-glob`, `-regexp`, `-nocase`, fall-through or `case`
  statement stays one statement of the CFG with its arm bodies inline, so no
  block held a write inside one, and every reader of the lattice saw
  `set go 1; switch -glob -- [gets stdin] { q* { set go 0 } }` leave `go` at
  1: W241 on `while {$go} {…}`, W240 on the twin that starts `go` at 0, an
  O102 fold of `puts $go` to `puts 1`, an I230 that `if {$go}` is always
  true, an O112 fold, and iRules flow checks that never reached a `respond`
  under `if {$is_api}`. The hole is closed where the lattice is built, not in
  its consumers. `ssa::switch_may_defs` (beside `defs_of_with_registry`)
  walks every arm, the default and every command they nest — a statement's
  own writes, the variable a `regexp` or `scan` fills, a `global`, `upvar` or
  `variable` binding, the commands of a `[…]` substitution in a word — and
  returns each name any of them may write that the statement does not define
  on every path. Each is a *may*-def: `rename_statement` gives it a version
  whose prior one is recorded as a use, so the solver joins the version from
  before the statement with one that has no value, the merged value is not
  constant, and the existence rung reads it as unknown afterwards — for a
  place unbound before the switch too. The same set reaches the analyses
  that walked the graph's blocks: the taint join (`propagate_statement_taints`
  keeps the taint a name held when no arm runs), the alias lattice
  (`stmt_gen` applies a `global`, `upvar` or `variable` inside an arm as if it
  had run, a union, which is the may-alias answer) and W210's undefined-read
  walk (`MayDefMap`, `UndefIndexMaps` and `UndefWalk` read a may-def as a
  one-operand phi, so `switch -glob $x { a* { set v 1 } }; puts $v` still
  reports `v` possibly unset). The CFG builder asks what it would have put
  beside each command an arm runs had it lowered the arm
  (`CfgBuilder::opaque_arm_effects`, through `apply_upvar_invalidation`, which
  records the function-level facts too): the names a callee writes into the
  frame (`proc zero {v} {upvar 1 $v x; set x 0}` called as `zero go` in an
  arm) become the may-definitions of a marker statement after the `switch`
  (`SyntheticMarker::ArmWrites`, read by `switch_may_defs` as the `switch`'s
  own writes are, and skipped by codegen and the wasm plan); a command that may
  write any name (`namespace eval`, `dict with`, `eval $script`, a callee that
  aliases a computed name) adds the caller-frame barrier the graph puts after
  such a command it lowers, unless the command leaves the procedure. Where the
  selection record proves which body runs, the write could be exact; that
  precision is not built, and the answer is the may-def's.
- **D194 — A callback script's writes escape as a trace's do** (review fix
  1, B1). `after 100 { set done 1 }`, `after idle { set ::go 0 }`, `bind`,
  `fileevent` and `chan event`, `interp bgerror` and the script of a
  `trace add` run after the registering command returns, at the global level
  or in the frame of whatever fires them, so the name they write is one the
  registering code holds and nothing in its text shows the write: `set done
  0; after 100 { set done 1 }; while {!$done} { update }` drew W240, and the
  `::go` twin W241. The registry states which stored scripts are callbacks
  and the compiler names no command. `Traits::BODY_RUNS_IN_OWN_FRAME` (new;
  `fields.md` lists it) marks the definers — `proc`, an iRules `when`,
  `snit::method`, `snit::typemethod`, the snit macro, `optproc`, `lambda`,
  `report::defstyle` — whose stored script is dormant like a callback's
  (`DEFERS_BODY`) but runs in a frame of its own, and
  `CommandRegistry::callback_script_indices(name, args, dialect)` returns
  the words `script_timing` calls `Deferred`, less those of a command
  carrying it. An unset flag keeps the abstaining answer, a callback, so a
  pack's own definer states the trait to opt out and is sound without it.
  `deferred_writes::scan_module` (one pass over the lowered module, filling
  `Module.deferred_writes`, a `DeferredWrites { names, any }`) reads each
  registration's callback words: a literal script is lowered and every name
  its statements may write is recorded (a plain name with `::` stripped, an
  array's base name, a `global`, `upvar` or `variable` binding, the writes of
  a nested substitution); a word naming a procedure of the module adds the
  global names that procedure writes; a write whose name the callback
  computes (`set $n 1`), or a procedure that writes through a frame it cannot
  name, sets `any`, which reads every variable as written. A quoted word with
  no substitution is read as the script it is, and a word that is one `[…]`
  substitution of a command the registry states builds a command prefix
  (`Traits::BUILDS_COMMAND_PREFIX`: `list`) is read as the command it builds
  (`after 100 [list tick $n]`, `-command [list set done 1]`). A callback word
  that is otherwise computed (`after 100 $script`), spelled as several words
  (`after 100 set done 1`, where the registry states no script position) or
  expanded is not read: the text is unknown, so a write it makes stays
  invisible, a limit the design page states. The names join the escaping
  names exactly as `traced_variables` do — `sccp::escaping_names` through
  `TraceInputs::deferred_writes`, O102's `extend_module_escaping`, the type
  pass's escape set, the existence rung's `dynamic_trace` — and stay a fact
  of their own because the taint lattice
  reads `traced_variables` as tainted everywhere. They reach the
  per-procedure memo identity (`AnalysisContextKey::deferred_writes`) and the
  database's `ModuleTraceFacts`, so editing a callback invalidates the checks
  that read it; `compiler_check_memo_matches_uncached_for_hidden_writes` pins
  the memoised and uncached answers equal.
- **D195 — A top-level name and its `::` spelling agree across a call the
  module cannot see** (review fix 1, B1). `set g 5; foo; if {$g} {…}`
  folded the `if` and drew I230 where `set ::g 5; foo; if {$g} {…}` did not:
  a qualified global was externally mutable, a plain name at the top level
  was refined, although that name *is* the global and `foo`, which the module
  cannot see (`ModuleCommandBindings::may_dispatch_unresolved`: a literal
  head neither in the registry for the dialect nor bound by the module), may
  write it. The CFG builder marks such a call — its own head, a `[…]`
  substitution in one of its words, in a condition, or in an arm of an opaque
  `switch` — with a synthetic statement carrying
  `SyntheticMarker::UnseenCall`, only outside a procedure body, where a plain
  name is a local no callee reaches. The SSA rename records, where the marker
  stands, each version live there (`SsaFunction::unseen_call_versions`,
  `is_observed_by_unseen_call`). The solver treats the definition of a
  recorded version as possibly replaced — `Overdefined`, and so a phi over

  (`statement_clobber`), and O102 forwards no value of a recorded version and

  typed `CommandTokens::synthetic`, never its spelling, and `unit_scope`'s

  widened every top-level name function-wide behind a flag; it made
  `propagate_types` and O125 widen values nothing had written, failed 27

  widening is per version: a use before the call of a recorded version is
  undecided as well, which costs precision, not soundness. A call that

- **D196 — IRULE4004 counts the writes of a `switch` arm the graph keeps
  whole** (review fix 1, B2). `find_hoistable_set_warnings` counts every write
  of every event, so that a second write anywhere disqualifies the first, and

- **D197 — The flattened chain compares the values of a `switch`'s words**
  (review fix 2, B3). The statement records each word as a spelling with its

  newline pattern) are each tests, and six more were found beside them: a

  and was right, and left it a spelling on the chain, which was not; one test

- **D198 — A subject an option scan may read is not flattened** (review fix
  2, S1). Before 8.5 `Tcl_SwitchObjCmd` scans every leading word that starts
  with `-` as an option, however many words follow; from 8.5 it stops with two
  left. So `set x -glob; switch $x {-glob {puts G} default {puts D}}` raises

  unless `--` ended the run (`bounded_scan`). The two words the 8.5 scan leaves

  {puts D}` is `extra switch pattern with no body` from 8.4 to 9.1 — and only

  through the core's own option scan (`parse_options`, which must find the
  subject where the plan put it), so it already declined the words form on every

  `cfg_lower::subject_may_scan_as_option`, which `cfg_builder::switch_is_flattened`
  now takes with the statement, the registry and the lexer config: a registry

  one option parser (`parse_switch_options`, which now reports whether `--`

  that does not start with `-` folds through it (O112 and the arms never

  value that does is declined. The optimiser's `decided` no longer asks the

- **D199 — I231 names the command its statement spells** (review fix 3, N1). The
  message opened `Switch arm '…' is never selected` for every case-list
  statement, and a `case` statement is another command, with its own contract
  and gone from 9.0. `Statement::Switch` records the source's spelling in

- **D200 — The Explorer's post-SSA card words a branch fact by its kind and

  `constantBranches` entry `block: condition is always value (take target)`,

- **D201 — Code, test and design-page text states the rule, not the lane's
  bookkeeping** (review fix 3, S2 and S3). A comment that cites a decision, an

  at nothing. Each line `grep -nE 'D1[5-9][0-9]|VT[0-9]\.[0-9]|slice [0-9]'
  rust/` found says what the code does in words, as do the comments that cited
  the lane document or an earlier decision by number, except what a gate or a
  syntax needs in that form: the `registry-axis-ok … until slice N` waiver

  hex constant and the `RIPEMD160` command names. The design pages state the
  design as it is: a passage that dated built behaviour by the slice that built
  it ("until slice 5", "since slice 8 (VT8.5)") is in the present tense, and the

Taken while slice 9 was resumed on the reworked tree (§ *Slice 9* › *Record
(2026-09-30): slice 9* has the witnesses):

- **D202 — A statement's words read a place its own substitutions write before, between and after the write** (VT9.3). The SSA gives a statement one version of a name, and the call the CFG builder puts ahead of a statement for the writes of its `[…]` words defines each place they name, so the statement's own read named the version after the write, though the first word of `$x + [set x 10] + $x` reads the version before it. Nothing read the version before, and the store feeding it looked overwritten: O109 deleted `set x 1` ahead of `puts [expr {$x + [set x 10] + $x}]`, `set r [expr {…}]`, `expr {…}`, `return [expr {…}]`, `incr y [expr {…}]`, an `if` condition and a `while` condition, and the optimised program raised `can't read "x"` where tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 print `21` and `10`; where the write was an `incr`, which reads its target, O102 forwarded the version before the write into each `$x` word of `foo $x [incr x] $x` and printed `1 2 1` where tclsh prints `1 2 2`. The order of the words inside a statement is not modelled, so the answer does not rest on it: the call that carries the write reads the version before it, by name, for every place a word of the statement reads (D203), so the store feeding the first word stays; and no word of the statement is an operand something may rewrite, because which version a word names cannot be told — the host's use of such a place is a by-name use (`demote_reads_beside_writes`, run over each block's effect calls and the statement after each, which is D192's pairing) and a `Call`'s use is one too (D204). The price is precision where the answer was already approximate: a word that does run ahead of the write is no longer forwarded the earlier value. A place no word reads is not read by the call, so `puts [set x 2]` and a `while {[gets $fd line] >= 0}` leave the store before them dead, and O109, O126, W220 and W211 still say so. A first version had the call read every place it defines, which needs no scan of the statement; it was dropped because it made those two stores live.
- **D203 — What the carrying call reads is told from every read the statement makes** (VT9.3). The statement's own uses leave out the reads that sit where the lowering keeps no word structure — an expression's `ExprNode::Command` is one spelling, an `incr` amount is a string — and the commands a `[…]` word runs read variables of their own, so a place read only inside `[string length $x]`, or inside the braced expression of `[expr {$x + 1}]`, beside a write of it would feed nothing. `ir_helpers::statement_substituted_reads` and `condition_substituted_reads` take the statement's uses, the text of every substitution surface and the brace-quoted expression words the substitution recovery descends (`EvaluatedCommandSubstitutions::in_frame_expression_texts`, new), scan each as a word, and `CfgBuilder::read_beside_writes` matches them to the places the substitutions write by base name (an element and its array, a `::` spelling and the plain one). The scan runs only for a statement whose substitutions write something, which is the rare one. It is not a general recovery of the reads inside a command substitution: where nothing writes the place, found and left (§ *Green at VT9.3*).
- **D204 — A `Call` reads the places it holds beside an embedded write by name** (VT9.3). A `Call` host holds its embedded writes in its own `defs` and the carrying call's reads in its own `reads`, with no call of its own, so `uses_in_call` had the same two defects at one statement: its final filter dropped a word's read of a place the call defines, and a place also read before it is written kept its words as operands (`foo $x [incr x] $x`). A name in both `reads` and `defs` is one the call's embedded commands write: the lowering puts a command's own target in `reads` only where the registry gives its position a `VarRead` role, which `lappend` and `append` do not give theirs, and W210's `embedded_cell_update_read` rests on the same fact. A word of such a place is read by name, so `lappend l [incr n] $n` forwards nothing into `$n`, while `lappend l $l` still forwards `$l`, which is read before `lappend` writes it.

Taken in the second review of slice 6 (§ *Slice 6* › *Record (2026-09-30):
review fixes for slice 6*, round 2, has the witnesses):

- **D205 — An opaque `catch` and a deferred `try` state what their scripts write and run as an opaque `switch` does** (round 2, B1). The statement keeps its scripts inside itself, so the scans of the statements the graph lowers never reached a command in one: the `UnseenCall` marker, the barrier and the callee writes an opaque `switch` had were missing, and the `catch` call listed the names its body writes among its own definitions, which every path makes, though the body stops at its first error — `set g 5; catch { if {…} { set g 0 } }; puts $g` had W220 and O109 call `set g 5` dead, and `catch { namespace eval :: {set go 0} }` left I230 on `if {$go}`. `opaque_script_effects` is the one walk, for a `switch`'s arms (`opaque_arm_effects`), a `catch` body and a `try`'s body, handlers and `finally` script: each nested statement is asked `apply_upvar_invalidation`, the names a callee writes join the statement's own writes (`ssa::nested_writes`), and what comes out is one `ArmWrites` marker, the `CallerFrameOpaque` barrier and the `UnseenCall` marker, all ahead of the call, because the body runs before the call assigns its result variable and the marker must see the versions before it. The inlined `catch`, whose exception edge leaves from before the body, already joined the version before the body with the one it writes, so this is the same may-definition and W210 reads it as a φ with one operand: a name only the body sets is reported where it is read, as after an inlined `catch`. Two differences from the `switch`: a command that leaves the procedure (`error`, `exit`, `return`) is no exemption from the barrier, since an error inside a `catch` or a `try` resumes after it (`leaves_the_procedure` is `false`), and the result and options variables stay definite definitions of the call. The deferred `try` is reached only by the codegen shape (`defer_top_level`); a handler's variables are may-definitions there because a handler runs only when it is selected.
- **D206 — A computed head is an unseen call, and a call's words are read before it may rewrite them** (round 2, B1). A computed head runs whatever its value names, so outside a procedure body, where a plain name is the global the code reaches, it is unseen as a literal head the module cannot resolve is (`call_is_unseen`); in a procedure it marks nothing, as a literal one does not. Recording the versions live at the marker forces them `Overdefined` wherever they are read, the head's own read included, so `set e c1; $e configure` and `foo$suffix` lost the resolution the analyser takes from the solver, and W123 and W307 drew on programs that name a created or defined command; the operands of the call lost theirs too (`set a 1; set b 2; set c 3; eval {$a $b $c}` no longer forwarded the constants). The call reads its words before its head runs, so the marker that follows a call takes the names those words read — the head, each word that is not brace-quoted and the commands such a word runs (`words_read_by_call`) — as its may-definitions, and the versions are recorded after them (`enrich_unseen_call_reads`, `RenameWalk::enter_block`): the version a word read is not recorded, and every later read is of a version the unseen call may have written. The rule is the call's, not the head's: a literal head the module cannot see (`foo $a`) and a `source` take it too, so an operand of one folds. The names are stated in the SSA, on the copy of the CFG the build reads, because a name stated on the marker in the CFG, which this commit first did with an `ArmWrites` marker for the head's variables, is a write to every pass that reads a call's `defs`: `unit_scope` took `set cmd foo; $cmd 1` for a variable written twice and stopped resolving the dispatch, and the instance-class state `taint` keeps lost the receiver of `set widget [ttk::entry .w]; $widget configure …`. A brace-quoted word is passed as it is and the code the call reaches may evaluate it later, so a name only it carries stays recorded; a store the callee may read is not dead, since the marker's use of the version before it keeps the store (`set a 1; set b 2; set c 3; eval {$a $b $c}` is `lassign {1 2 3} a b c` and `eval {1 2 3}`, the command `1` being one the module cannot see). The marker of an unseen command a substitution runs goes ahead of the host and follows no call, so it states no name, and a computed head inside a substitution does not resolve (found and left).
- **D207 — A substitution's commands are asked about unseen code through every word they run as code** (round 2, B1; round 3). `evaluated_command_substitutions` recovers the commands a statement's `[…]` words run and descends the expression words, never a body word, so `if {[catch {foo}]} …` and `puts [catch {foo}]` ran an unseen command no marker followed. `command_reaches_unseen` reads each recovered command and every word it runs as code, to the depth cap past which the text is taken to run anything: each `ArgRole::Body` word, whichever frame it runs in — the script of a `catch` or a loop, and the body of an `uplevel` or a `namespace eval`, which run in another (round 3: the first form read the registry's plain, same-frame body words alone, so `set g 5; set x [namespace eval ns {foo}]; if {$g} …` drew I230 and folded where tclsh prints `b` when `foo` sets `::g 0`); the body of a lambda literal (`ArgRole::LambdaLiteral`, the second element of its list, which `apply` has in place of a `Body` word); the commands in the text of a command that performs command substitution (`subst`, through `substitutions_performed`, which `-nocommands` empties); and those in an expression word (`ArgRole::Expr`, and every word of a command that concatenates its arguments into one expression: `catch {if {[foo]} …}`). A word that is computed (`catch $script`, `apply $lambda`) is unseen outside a procedure. A definition's body (`proc`) is read too, which marks a substitution that defines a procedure: sound, and a little imprecise. Only the marker is stated for these bodies: the names they write and the barriers they raise are not stated, in whichever frame they run (found and left, #2323: `set g 5; set rc [catch {set g 0}]; if {$g} …` still draws I230).
- **D208 — A callback the scan cannot read may write any variable** (round 2, B2). The scan answered "no write" for a callback it could not read, which is the unsound direction: a computed script can write anything. It sets `DeferredWrites::any`, which reads as a trace on a computed name, for a computed word at a callback position, a `[…]` word of a command that builds no command prefix (`command_prefix`), a `{*}` expansion in an invocation whose command stores a script (`expanded_registration`: the form the words before the expansion pick, or any form of the command when none is picked, with `DEFERS_BODY` and not `BODY_RUNS_IN_OWN_FRAME`), a computed command head or an expansion in a callback script, a plain body word of a callback script that is computed, and a command that is neither a procedure of the module nor a command of the registry the module leaves as it ships it. The last asks the module's command bindings (`ModuleCommandBindings`, taken the first time it is needed): one target, the registry's own descriptor of that spelling, no argument an `interp alias` prepends; an alias, a rename, a widget path and a spelling nothing defines are not read, so a file that stores a callback it does not define is undecided throughout, as `after 100 $script` is. A nested registration in a callback script (`after 1 {after 1 set done 1}`) is read the way a statement's is (`callbacks`), its plain body words once. The cost is precision where the module stores a callback to a command another file defines.
- **D209 — A callback spelled as several words is read through the registry's one-word form** (round 2, B2). `after ms script script …` joins its words as `concat` does, and the registry names a callback position only for the form with one script word, because marking the first of several would arity-check a truncated fragment. The scan asks again: for each split of the invocation's words it joins the tail into one word (`concat_words`: each word trimmed of white space, the empty ones dropped, one space between) and asks `callback_script_indices` for that shape; the first split at which the position of the joined word is named is the script, read as one, or a callback the scan cannot read when a word of the tail is not literal. An invocation that stores nothing (`after cancel …`, `after info`, a delay alone) names no position at any split and is left alone. No command name is written in the scan; the registry's own resolver is the one place that says which form has a script.
- **D210 — W220 and W211 read the unseen-call record O109 and O126 read** (round 2, S1). A call to a command the module cannot see may read the name a store leaves, so a store before it is no dead store (W220) and a name some version of which it holds is no unused variable (W211): the two diagnostics asserted what the optimiser, which asked `SsaFunction::name_is_observed_by_unseen_call`, did not act on. A name's W211 is per variable, so any version it holds at such a call exempts every chain of it; a store after the last call has none to read it and is still reported.
- **D211 — A list element decodes under the document's escapes, in the lowering and in the selection** (round 2, S2). Before 8.6 a `\x` takes every hex digit that follows and keeps the last two, so the element `a\x41b` of a braced arm list is `a` and U+001B under 8.4 and 8.5 and `aAb` from 8.6, and the elements of a bare or quoted word are decoded where the list is split. The lowering split a braced arm list with the default decoder (`switch_body_elements`), which is what the flattened chain compares; the opaque forms' selection record splits the same list text again in `ConstOps::list_elements`, under the default grammar too, so the `-glob` form folded to `hit` under 8.4 and 8.5 as well, which the review's one-line fix did not reach. `tcl_syntax::list::split_list_in` takes the `EscapeSyntax` (`split_list` is its default); the lowering passes the lexer's, `ConstOps` the target profile's. A profile that names no release decodes as the default, as the lexer reads the same bytes in a word of such a document.
- **D212 — `catch` writes its result and options variables as nothing known** (round 2). The type pass stores the command's return value in the one variable a call without a typing override writes, and a call that writes several stays unknown; `catch` returns the integer completion code and writes the script's result and an options dictionary. The multi-definition guard was what kept an opaque `catch` clear of type findings on a result variable (an S100 for a list or a dictionary command over it), because its call listed its body's writes beside the result variable; now that the call defines its result and options variables alone, `catch {foo} msg` would type `msg` as an integer, as it did when the body wrote nothing. The registry's entry declares `VarWriteTyping::Destructured`, which is the answer for a command whose variables are not its return value, and the guard stays for the commands that have no override.

Taken while the lattice learnt a statement's nested writes (§ *Slice 9* › *Record (2026-09-30): slice 9* has the witnesses):

- **D213 — A statement's substitutions are evaluated once, as the call that carries their writes and the host that takes the result** (VT9.2). The CFG builder puts a synthetic `<upvar-invalidate>` call ahead of a host statement whose `[…]` words write something, and the SSA gives the call the definitions the words make and the host the result. The solver gave the call's definitions no value and evaluated the host under the effect-free policy, which declines a nested write (`StatefulNested`), so `$x + [incr x] + $x` was no constant and nothing after it was forwarded. `sccp_process_statements` asks `LatticeDriver::evaluate_embedded` at the call, which finds the host (`ssa::effect_call_host`: D192's adjacency and span, shared with `demote_reads_beside_writes`) and evaluates the two once under `NestedPolicy::LocalWrites`, from the versions the pair reads (`incoming_versions`: the host's uses, the call's, and each place the call defines at the version ahead of the call, because the host's own use of such a place names the call's definition, which is what is being computed; a place no definition and no root value has there is read as unknown rather than waited for). The host is an `AssignExpr` or an `ExprEval`, whose parsed expression the engine runs, or an `AssignValue` whose word is one `[expr …]` substitution (`ordered_script`: `[a][b]` is two substitutions and keeps the effect-free policy). For each member of the finite input the call's definitions take the last write the state holds per place, and a place no write reached `Preserve`s, so `0 && [incr x]` leaves `x#2` the value of `x#1` and `SccpResult::preserved` says so (`embedded_defs`, over `defs_from_placed`, which `apply_outcome`'s definition loop shares); the members join, and the host's definition takes the result and its folded type. The host's answer waits in `sccp_process_statements` for its own statement. What the evaluation cannot own keeps the answers the pair had: a write to a place the call does not define, a cell written beside the array that holds it, an error completion (the prefix rule publishes only the writes it ran, which a definition cannot state; no route yields one yet), and a host that is a `Call` (`puts [expr {…}]`), a `Return`, a condition or a value that is any other command, which keep `EffectFreeOnly`. `set x 1; set r [expr {$x + [incr x] + $x}]` gives `r` 5 and `x` 2, and the values O100 forwards from those definitions are the nested store's; O102's conditions and O109's guards are those of D202 to D204, so the statement's own `$x` is still no operand to forward and the store feeding it stays.
- **D214 — A command's own substituting words run before it, in order, under one state** (VT9.2). Tcl substitutes a command's words from left to right and then runs it, so what one word's commands write is seen by the next word and by everything the command reads. The first form of D213 evaluated each word of a nested command on its own, and a 45-program differential corpus run through `tcl opt` under tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 found `set s a; set r [expr {[string length $s] + [string length [append s bc]]}]; puts "$r $s"` printing `4 a` where tclsh prints `4 abc` (and the same for `lappend`): the write the `append` word made was the word's, which `string length` never carried to the statement. Under `LocalWrites`, `run_script` gives the command's `LatticeInputs` `Words::Ordered`: every operand that substitutes is evaluated once, in operand order, under one state, when the first is read (`ordered_word`, `evaluate_words`; `substituted_in` reads a variable from the state's writes before the lattice and joins a command's writes into the state), and every route reads all its operands before it reads a cell (`evaluate_lifted` pins them first), so the words have run before anything reads what they wrote. The route's reads of a cell — `prior_store` and the existence read — consult those writes first, and `carrying_word_writes` puts them ahead of an outcome's own for every route but the expression engine, which starts its state from them (`AnalysisInputs::word_state`, defaulted `None`, forwarded by `PinnedInputs`), joins the evidence they rest on, and counts them in an error completion's prefix. A quoted operand of `expr` is one such word, so `expr "$x + [incr x]"` is `1 + 2` however often the engine reads it, and an operand the engine substitutes itself — `expr {$x} + [incr x]`, joined into `$x + 2` — is read after every word has run, as Tcl does. A command whose words are independent (`Words::Independent`, the effect-free policy) answers exactly as before.

Taken in the third review fixes of slice 6 (§ *Slice 6* › *Record (2026-09-30): review fixes for slice 6*, round 3, has the witnesses):

- **D215 — A read after code the module cannot see is no read before it is set, for a name nothing in the function assigns** (round 3). The marker for unseen code (D195) may-defines the names that have a version where it sits, and records them (`SsaFunction::unseen_call_versions`), so a name with no version yet has nothing for it to record: `source other.tcl; puts $g`, `foo; puts $g`, `$cmd; puts $g` and `catch {foo}; puts $g` drew W210 on a read of a global the code may well have set, though the rule the marker is made under says the code may write any global. W210's walk of version-0 reads skips a read the marker precedes — earlier in its block or in a block that dominates the read, as `written_by_substitution_before` reads a substitution's write (`UndefSuppression::unseen_call_before`), the statement a substitution's marker stands ahead of included — and version 0 only: a name that has a definition keeps its W210 where a path leaves it unset. So a marker on one path only, a read in the statement of the call itself (`foo $g`, whose words are read before its head runs), a procedure's locals, which no callee reaches, and `puts $g` with no unseen code ahead of it still draw it, and a `source` in a procedure, which runs in the frame of the call, silences it there. The marker's own definitions are not changed: for every other consumer a read of a name with no version stays a read of the undefined root, whose answers already allow for code that sets it (the value is overdefined and an existence check is not folded).

Taken in slice 10, completion paths (§ *Slice 10* › *Record (2026-10-01): slice 10* has the witnesses):

- **D216 — An error a route proves is a completion, after the stores that ran** (VT10.1). A core's `CmdError` or `ValueError` was a decline, so a statement the route proved to raise had every definition `Overdefined` and the prefix rule had nothing to publish. `ConstOps` now keeps the program's error beside the decline a failed call answers with (`ConstOps::decline` and `decline_value` return the same `WrongRepresentation` as before, and record a `Raised`), and a route that models completions asks for it (`ConstOps::raised`): `stopped` answers the error with `written: 0` where the failure came before any store (`cell_update`, `keyed_update`, `string range`, `list`, `llength`, `string length`, `lassign`'s and `array set`'s list, `regexp`'s and `regsub`'s pattern), and `Publication::publish` answers `Error { written: k }` where a store reaches a place the analysis proves holds an array (`ArrayWrite::array_place`: the existence fact is `Bound(Array)`, and an element, a place of another kind or a fact the rung does not state is no proof): every store stays listed in order, the places after the failing one keep what they held, and only the stores that ran have a type. A kind that is not proven is no error, so the normal answers are byte-identical. A route that does not ask keeps the decline.
- **D217 — A message and an `-errorcode` are exact only where every release the target names words them alike** (VT10.1). `Raised::unanimous` runs the wording per release (the named one, or `TclVersion::ALL`) and keeps each field the releases agree on and leaves the other `ExactValueOrUnavailable::unproven_string()`, a bound string with no text. The wordings are the measured ones (tclsh 8.4.20, 8.5.19, 8.6.18, 9.0.4, 9.1b0). Writing to an array: `set`, `append`, `lappend`, `lassign` and `binary scan` say `can't set "b": variable is array` in every release, `scan`, `regexp` and `regsub` say `couldn't set variable "b"` up to 8.5, and `incr` says `can't read "b": variable is array` under 8.4; the code is `NONE` before 8.6 and `TCL WRITE VARNAME` from it. An absent name: `unset` says `can't unset "x": no such variable` and a read of one (`set x`) says `can't read "x": no such variable`, with `NONE` before 8.6 and `TCL LOOKUP VARNAME x` from it; 8.4's `incr` of one says the second with `NONE`; a whole array read as a scalar says `can't read "b": variable is array`, with `NONE` and from 8.6 `TCL READ VARNAME`. An element's message and code say whether its array exists (`TCL LOOKUP VARNAME a` where it does not, `TCL READ VARNAME` where the element does not), which the fact does not, so an element's error is certain and its wording unproven. A bad index: `bad index "x": must be integer or end?-integer?` under 8.4 and `…integer?[+-]integer? or end?[+-]integer?` from 8.5, `NONE` and from 8.6 `TCL VALUE INDEX`. A list that does not split: the parser's message in every release (`ListError::from_message` names the failure; the core raises the message alone), `NONE` and from 8.6 `TCL VALUE LIST BRACE`, `QUOTE` or `JUNK`; an odd dictionary, `missing value to go with key` and `TCL VALUE DICTIONARY` from 8.6; an odd `array set` list, `list must have an even number of elements` and `TCL ARGUMENT FORMAT` from 8.6. `error message ?info? ?code?` raises its first word and, as the code, its third or `NONE`. The interface page's "the code is exact in every case" is the plan's rule read through the table above: the code differs by release too, so a profile that names no release proves a message the releases share and none of the codes.
- **D218 — A limit of the model is no error the program raises** (VT10.1). `ValueError::IntegerOverflow` is a value 8.4 wraps and 8.5 widens, an inadmissible axis and a budget are the evaluation's own faults, and a release the target leaves ambiguous is no answer: each stays a decline, and a fault recorded at any point of a run wins over an error recorded before it (`ConstOps::raised` answers nothing once a fault is set). Only the failures a core reports for a program's own input are errors: a value that reads as no integer, double or boolean, a list that does not split, a malformed index, a name that is absent or an array.
- **D219 — `error` and `unset` have routes** (VT10.1). `error message ?info? ?code?` (`completion.rs`, new; `NativeEvalId::ErrorRaise`) is the first command whose every evaluation is an error completion, after no store; a word the analysis does not prove leaves its field unproven and the completion certain. `unset` (`NativeEvalId::VariableUnset`, replacing the derived descriptor's no-route) unbinds in order and raises on the first name the rung proves unbound, unless `-nocomplain` is given: the names before it are unbound, it and the names after it are not touched, and a name an earlier word of the command unset is absent by then; an element, and a name whose existence the rung does not prove, decline.
- **D220 — An integer division or remainder by zero in an expression is an exact error** (VT10.1). `ExprServices::arith` ends the evaluation with `divide by zero` and `-errorcode` `ARITH DIVZERO {divide by zero}`, which every release words alike, counting the writes the expression's commands had made; an operand that is a float makes the operation floating point (`1 / 0.0` is `Inf`), and one that reads as no integer raises another error the engine does not word, so both keep their old answers.
- **D221 — `format` and `binary format` keep declining on a core error** (VT10.1, a departure from "every registry-owned route"). `format` runs each release apart and compares the answers, so an error in some and not in others is ambiguity, not an error, and the combination of per-release wording is not built; `binary format` declines the fields its releases differ on one by one and leaves the packer's own refusals as declines, none of which is measured to be every release's. Neither statement was an error before, and neither is now.
- **D222 — A statement that certainly raises, where a handler is thrown to, publishes the stores that ran and has no way out but the exception edge** (VT10.2). A block that is a source of a handler's exception edge — the body of a flattened `catch` (D223), the body of a `try` in the faithful build — is where a throw leaves from (`RegionShape::throwing`; the driver is told, `set_throwing`). There the driver evaluates every statement for whether it raises, whatever its definitions need (`probe_completion` for one that defines nothing), and a statement whose every outcome is an `Error { written }` answers `DefValues::Raised`: its definitions are those of the stores that ran (`raised_defs`: the placed stores up to `written`, every place they did not reach preserved — `b(k)` over an array `b` keeps its value — and the members of a finite input joined), its block has no normal way out (`BlockExit::completes`: the terminator opens the exception edges alone), and each later statement of the block is not run: its definitions keep what their places held and its existence is left as it was (`keep_prior`). Outside such a block — an error with no handler to take it — a statement widens as before, so no code is proven unreachable by an error the procedure raises itself and no diagnostic gains a reason from one (B-DP4).
- **D223 — A flattened `catch` body is a block per statement in the analysis build, so the handler is thrown to from between its stores** (VT10.2). `lower_catch` asks `lower_script` to end a block after each statement but the last (`split_script`, `split_blocks`), and each of those blocks, the block before the body and the tail are exception-edge sources to the end block. The end block had been thrown to from the block before the body and the tail alone, so a handler saw the state before the body and at its end and never the one between two stores: `set x 1; catch {set x 2; foo; set x 1}; puts $x` printed `1` once optimised where tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 print `2` (O109 deleted `set x 2`), and `set a 2` in the like program `a=3` for `a=2`. The codegen build keeps the body in the one block its inline emitter compiles, so its bytecode is as it was and its `region_entries` are empty.
- **D224 — The edge from the block before a body is a region entry, which the solver opens when the body's first command can fail before it stores** (VT10.2). `Function::region_entries` lists the exception edges from the block before a flattened `catch` or `try` body to its handler with the block that holds the body's first command (`RegionEntry`; `lower_catch` and `push_try_handler_exception_edges` record them). Such an edge carries the exit of the block before the body, and it opens when its first command is processed and does not raise only after a store (`BlockExit::entry_throws`: false where the command certainly raises after at least one store, as `lassign {new second} a b` over an array `b` does, so the handler sees `a` at `new` and never at `old`). The existence rung's handler regions leave the block before the body out, so the handler takes that state at its exit through the edge and not at every point inside the block; a body that cannot fall through has no such edge, and the state its first block entered with is among its region's points, joined unless the first command raises only after a store (`ExistenceAt::leave`).
- **D225 — A `try` body of one block publishes the prefix as a `catch` body does; a body of several statements is VT10.5's** (VT10.2). `lower_try` does not split its body, so what a `try` body stores between two commands is not a state its handler sees: `proc foo {} {error x}; proc p {} {set x 1; try {set x 2; foo; set x 1} on error {} {}; puts $x}` is optimised to print `1` where tclsh 8.6 to 9.1 print `2`, as `catch` did before D223. VT10.5 gives a `try` body the same blocks and edges; `a_throw_between_two_writes_is_a_state_the_handler_sees` holds the program in a `catch` until then.
- **D226 — An error in a word is an error before the command** (VT10.2). Tcl substitutes every word of a command before it runs it, so `append x 2 [error boom]` stores nothing and `set r [expr {1 + [error mid]}]` leaves `r` unbound, and the handler is thrown to with the state before the statement. The driver notes when a nested command of a word answers an error (`word_error`), and a statement whose evaluation then declined is `Raised` with no stores (`prefix: None`): every definition keeps what its place held, a typed assignment's existence included (`ExistenceAt::step_for`).
- **D227 — A pair of an embedded call and its host that certainly raises gives the writes it made** (VT10.2). Slice 9's pair (`evaluate_embedded`) declined when an outcome was an error. Where a throw leaves from and every outcome is one, the call's definitions are the writes the expression's commands made before the error (`EmbeddedAnswer::raised`) and the host's keep what they held: in a procedure `catch {set r [expr {[incr x] + [error mid]}]}` leaves `x` at 2, which restates the seventh ordered-state witness (`x#2` is `const(2)`, `Overdefined` before), and at the top level, where the `catch` is one call, `x` is still unknown. Elsewhere the pair is not evaluated.
- **D228 — `catch` declares its semantics: an existence transfer and no route** (VT10.2, a departure from the plan's order). `CatchSemantics` (`completion.rs`) binds the result and options variables as scalars on one path whose completion domain is any — whatever the script's completion they are written — and states nothing of what they hold: an opaque body's result variable is a write of a value that is not available, as the page says. It has no route (`none: unauthored`; evaluating a closed body is VT10.3's), and declaring it removes `catch` from `KNOWN_GAPS` here, since the gate counts a declared command no gap: the row VT10.3's plan removes goes with this item.
- **D229 — `lassign` lists its completion paths, and the solver reads only the evaluation's** (VT10.2). `ordered_writes_transfer` (`publication.rs`) is the existence transfer of a command that stores to its `VarWrite` operands in order: the normal path binds every target and is absent where one is certainly an array; the error path, present where a store may fail, binds the targets before the first one not proven writable as scalars and may-binds that one and the rest, or leaves them untouched where it is certainly an array. The Explorer's SCCP view lists for each statement what it stores on each completion path (`paths`: the evaluation's outcomes and, for a kind of completion the evaluation did not report, the transfer's). The solver applies the normal path's outcomes and the evaluation's own errors (D222) and does not read the transfer's error path: the state before a failing store is a throw source's exit or a point of its block, which the handler's join already holds.
- **D230 — `catch` evaluates a closed body in five commits, not one** (VT10.3). The plan gives VT10.3 `CatchSemantics` and the code table, in the registry alone. Reading the code first showed that its exit — `set c [catch {error boom} m]` printing `c#1 = const(1)`, `m#1 = const('boom')` and a `route catch:` line answering `evaluated` — and #2231 need five more things, each a commit with its own tests (rows VT10.3a to VT10.3e): (a) `return`, `break` and `continue` have no route (`NativeEvalId` ends at `ErrorRaise`) and `CompletionOutcome::Code` has no reader, so no body that completes with a code can be evaluated; (b) a nested `[catch {…}]` is not descended (`walk_braced_expr_words` takes `Expr` words, never `Body`), so the body's writes and the names it reads by name never reach the statement's effect call: `set x 1; set c [catch {incr x}]; if {$x == 2} …` and `[catch {append x y}]` keep the value `x` held before the body, and the passes rewrite on it (the statement form, `catch {incr x} m`, already states its body's writes as may-definitions and reads its names, D205, and was no part of the defect, though #2231 lists it); the descent follows the clause grammar's protected script (`ClauseTiming::Protected`, which `catch` and `try`'s body declare), never the command's name (R1); (c) the nested service evaluates one command and refuses a completion that is neither normal nor an error (`admitted_writes`), and `LatticeInputs::body` is `Unsupported`, so `NestedPolicy::Protected` runs a script's commands in order under one state, each exact and single-valued, and hands the first completion that is not a normal one to its caller, and `CatchSemantics` gets the route over it; (d) `ordered_script` evaluates a host that is one command substitution only where the route is the expression engine's, so the pair of a statement's effect call and its host takes any registry-owned direct route; (e) the flattened `catch` of a procedure's straight-line body parks its result and options variables on a marker with no words (`is_catch_defs_marker`, which codegen skips), so it cannot be evaluated where it stands, and the state at its end is not the state at its entry; its words ride on the analysis build's CFG and the marker is evaluated over the entry state of the region, with codegen's marker unchanged. The order is (a), (b), (c), (d), (e): (b) is a soundness repair that needs no evaluation, and (c) reads the names (b) records. The plan's code-table row `return -code 5 custom` in a procedure is a procedure call's completion, which needs the callee's summary (slice 13); tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 give `catch {return -code 5 custom}` the code 2 with the options `-code 5 -level 1`, and `catch {p}` over `proc p {} {return -code 5 custom}` the code 5, so the table row is the direct form and the procedure form is a witness that stays unknown.
- **D231 — A `Code` completion is the return options' `-code` and `-level`, and `return` evaluates only what every release reads alike** (VT10.3a). `CompletionOutcome::Code { code, level, result }` had no reader. It states what `return -code C -level L result` carries, so `catch` over it reports `TCL_RETURN` (2) while `L` is positive and `C` at level 0, with the options `-code C -level L`: tclsh 8.5 to 9.0 give `catch {return 5}` 2 with `-code 0 -level 1`, `catch {return -code 5 custom}` 2 with `-code 5 -level 1`, `catch {break}` 3 with `-code 3 -level 0`, and `return -code error boom` carries `-errorcode NONE` as well. `ReturnSemantics` reads the options as Tcl does, in pairs while two words remain and a last word on its own the result whatever it starts with, and reads `-code` and `-level` alone. Declined: any other option, which 8.5 keeps in the options dictionary and 8.4 refuses; a code or level not spelled in canonical decimal (`010` is 8 before 9.0 and 10 from it, `0x5` and `+5` read alike but are the release's grammar); a word that is not exact; and `-level` where the target is not proven to have it (from 8.5, `ReleaseAmbiguous` for a profile naming no release). At level 0 the code is the completion itself: `ok` a normal completion with the result, `error` the error with that message and `-errorcode` `NONE`. `break` and `continue` take no word (a word is `wrong # args`, which the route does not word) and complete with their code at level 0 and the empty result.
- **D232 — A protected script a substitution runs is the statement's effect, where it is brace-quoted text** (VT10.3b). The script of a `catch` and the body of a `try` run once, in the frame the substitution is written in, and what they complete with is observed rather than propagated, so the commands in them write and read this frame's names as a command written in the substitution does. The walk that recovers a statement's substituted commands already descended an expression word the same way (#2141, #2215); it now descends the words the clause plan places as `ClauseTiming::Protected`, whatever the command is called (R1), and the commands of that script, the expression words and protected scripts inside them, and the substitutions they hold. The two kinds of in-frame word share the lists they feed (`in_frame_commands` and `in_frame_texts`, renamed from the expression-only names) and the consumers that take them — the variable-effect view and the substituted reads — and the call-graph consumers (the `upvar` and global-write views) still do not take either. A script is known text only where it is brace-quoted: a quoted, computed or bracketed one (`catch "incr x"`, `catch $script`) is left as it was, since the text a second round of substitution reads is not the word's (corrected by D235: a quoted word that substitutes nothing is read, and any other is unreadable). Not descended: a handler and a `finally` of a `try` (a handler may not run, and `finally` is `Always`, not protected), and every other body a substitution runs — an `if` or `switch` arm, a loop, `eval`, `namespace eval`, `apply` — which runs zero or many times, in another frame or under names of its own, none of which a flat command list can say. That is the wider class of #2323 and it stays open: `set x 1; puts [foreach v 1 {incr x}]; puts $x` prints `1` optimised where tclsh prints `2`, and `set x 1; puts [eval {info exists x}]; set x 2` loses `set x 1`. The `catch` programs of #2323 (`set g 5; set rc [catch {set g 0}]; if {$g} …`, and the `fd` of `catch {set fd [open $f]} err`) are the same descent and are fixed with it.
- **D233 — A protected script is run whole, and `catch` is the route over it** (VT10.3c). `NestedPolicy::Protected` is the policy of a script whose completion its caller observes — `catch`'s, and later `try`'s body: its commands run in order under one state, each as under `LocalWrites`, and the first completion that is not the normal one is the script's, with the writes that ran before it in the state (an error counts every write the script made). A command that declines, a value that is not exact and a script that does not parse decline the whole, because the script's completion is the first of its commands that does not complete normally and each must be known to be past. `LatticeDriver::settle` is the post-processing every nested command shares, `admitted_writes` admits a `Code` completion when its command stored nothing of its own (`return`, `break` and `continue`: their words ran first), and the one command a substitution holds behaves as it did. A command in a protected script reads its roles from its words as a statement does (`resolve_roles_over_values`), or `set b $a` hid its target and declined. The flag a statement's word raising sets (`word_error`) is the statement's: the script runs with it cleared and restores it. `catch` evaluates where its script is brace-quoted text (`LatticeInputs::body`) and each variable word is a scalar or absent place the store succeeds on once the script has run (an element, a place that may be an array and one the script left unknown decline; a third word needs 8.5 and declines under 8.4, and under a profile naming no release). It completes normally with the code a caller of the script observes, writes the result variable what the script returned and the options variable a dictionary, and carries the script's writes as its own nested writes ahead of those two stores; `structure` is a body in the current frame with `CompletionProtocol::CatchAll`, and the existence transfer is unchanged. The options dictionary is never an exact value, so its store is `StoreOutcome::WriteUnavailable`, a write that certainly happened whose value is bounded and not spelled: a `MayWrite` would join the binding with what the place held and lose that `catch` binds it, and the same holds for a result the program does not prove. Measured under tclsh 8.5 to 9.1 (`the_options_dictionary_starts_with_the_code_and_level_the_route_states` runs every row on `PATH`): the dictionary begins `-code N -level L` for every completion but an error (`error msg info code` lists `-errorinfo` first), which is all the store states of its text — a prefix segment fact and type `dict` — and from 8.6 a normal completion is not always `-code 0 -level 0`: `catch {incr absent} m o` and `catch {lappend absent x} m o` leave `-errorcode {TCL READ VARNAME}` in `o` (8.5 leaves none), so the plan's "on success it holds `-code 0 -level 0`" holds as a prefix only. `::errorCode` and `::errorInfo` are not stated: they are `::`-qualified places the lattice never holds exact. A body that holds a `return` with options (`-code`, `-level`, `-options`) raises the caller-frame barrier before the opaque call, as `opaque_script_effects` does for a command that may write any name, which makes the result variable's existence unproven there; such a row evaluates in the nested form.
- **D234 — A command substitution that is a statement's whole value runs on whichever registry-owned route its command declares** (VT10.3d). D213's pair of a statement's effect call and its host ran the host's one command substitution under `LocalWrites` only where the command was on the expression engine's route: `ordered_script` refused every other, so `set c [catch {error boom} m]` kept `c` and `m` unknown though the route evaluates both, and `set a [incr n]` kept `n` and `a` unknown for the same reason. The refusal is gone: a `Direct` route — an evaluator the registry owns — runs as the expression route already did, its words' writes in order and its own stores after them, the call's definitions take what the state's writes left in each place, and the host takes the result and its folded type. The compiler names no command, so `incr`, `set`, `append`, `lappend`, `lassign`, `scan`, `regexp`, `dict set` and `catch` land their writes beside their result by the one rule. What it does not do: a host that is not an assignment — a `puts` argument, a `return`, a branch condition, so `if {[catch {…} m]} …` — keeps the effect-free policy; a head the module rebinds, an `Implementation` route and a command with no route are refused as before; a script that is not brace-quoted text stays unknown, as the `catch` route declines it (the 3c survivor, killed by the nested form's witness); and an outcome that is a code, not a normal completion or an error the pair publishes (D227), declines the pair. Two tests that pinned the effect-free reading are restated, not deleted: `a_value_position_set_reads_the_variable` (`[set x 10]` left its host no value; the host is now 10 and so is `x`) and `a_nested_catch_body_is_the_statements_effect` (a closed body now decides its condition, as tclsh decides it, where no diagnostic decided it; each program carries the truth of its condition and whether the analysis decides it, and a diagnostic that decides a condition the other way fails the test). Measured against tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 before the commit: an assignment's target word that substitutes (`set a([incr i]) [incr j]`) is outside the pair — the statement walk reads an assignment's value word only, so the call's definitions are the value word's and the target word's writes are in no definition, which is the case without the pair too (reported, below) — and a script word that is quoted or computed is outside the route (D232). Found while measuring, outside the plan, and reported to the coordinator rather than fixed: `set a([incr i]) 5` is deleted whole by O126 and `i` keeps the value it held, so `proc p {} {set i 0; set a([incr i]) 5; if {$i == 0} {return zero} else {return nonzero}}` returns `zero` optimised where it returns `nonzero`; O100's "Fold return of constant variable" rewrites `return "$r [string length abc]"` to `return 1` and `return "$r x"` to `return 1"` once `r` is a constant; and, inside D232's left-as-it-was, `proc p {} {set x 1; set c [catch "incr x"]; if {$x == 2} {return two} else {return other}}` and the same over `[catch $script]` return `two` where the optimised procedure returns `other`.
- **D235 — A protected script a substitution runs is read where its word is text, and unreadable where it is run-time data** (VT10.3b2; corrects D232). D232 left every script that is not brace-quoted as it was, on the reasoning that the text a second round of substitution reads is not the word's. Measured against tclsh 8.4 to 9.1 that was a miscompile, not a loss of precision: `proc p {} {set x 1; set c [catch "incr x"]; if {$x == 2} {return two} else {return other}}` returns `two`, and the optimised procedure returned `other`, and so did the same procedure over `[catch $script]`. The statement form raises a barrier for a body it cannot read (`catch with dynamic body`), and the substitution walk neither descended nor widened. The walk now reads a script's word by what it is. A brace-quoted word is the script. A quoted or bare word that substitutes nothing and holds no escape is the same text as written, and is descended as the braced one is: `[catch "incr x; set y 2"]` writes `x` and `y`. Any other word — a variable or command substitution, an expanded word, a word with an escape, which a second round reads differently from its source text — is run-time data: the script may write any name, so the walk is marked `opaque`, which puts the barrier ahead of the host as the statement form's does. Both come from the clause plan's protected clause, so a `try` body follows the same rule, and a handler and a `finally` are as D232 left them. A quoted script is still not run by the `catch` route (`LatticeInputs::body` accepts a brace-quoted word only, D234), so its writes are may-definitions and nothing after it is decided on a value from before it. The wider class of #2323 — an `if` or `switch` arm, a loop, `eval`, `namespace eval`, `apply` — is unchanged and stays open.
- **D236 — A flattened `catch` is evaluated where its region ends, over the state before its body, and the value its script ends with is observed** (VT10.3e). A `catch` in a procedure whose script is straight-line statements is lowered into blocks (`lower_catch`), and the statement that ends the region defines the result and options variables with no words of its own, which the code generator skips: the solver could only widen it. The analysis build now keeps the `catch` as written beside that statement (`Function::catch_ends`: the block before the body, the block that ends the region, and the call in the form the statement has when it is not flattened), and the codegen build keeps nothing, so the marker and the bytecode are as they were. The solver asks `LatticeDriver::evaluate_catch_end` at the marker, which runs the call through the route VT10.3c gave `catch` over the versions the block before the body exits with (`SsaBlock::exit_versions`), and takes the result and options variables' answers. The state before the body, not the state where the region ends, is the one the script runs over: over `x` = 1, `catch {incr x} m` leaves `m` 2 and `x` 2, where the joined state at the end would give an `incr` over 1 or 2. The script's own writes are not applied again, because its statements are in the flow and the solver has made them once. Found by the programs of this commit, and not an effect of the evaluation: the last command of a script is the value `catch` stores, so the last statement of a flattened body is observed where the region ends, and O126 had deleted it as a store nothing reads — `proc p {c} {catch {set v $c} m; puts "<$m>"}` printed `<>` optimised where tclsh prints `<7>`, and the same for a result variable that is a global or an `upvar` alias, an options variable beside it, and a `catch` in a branch; a result the lattice proved (`set v 1`) only hid it, by forwarding the value. The names the last statement stores now go to `alias_observed_vars`, the set O109 and O126 leave alone: a read on the marker would have made `set v …` read before it is set on the path where the body failed, a false W210, which that set was made to avoid. It costs precision, not soundness: every store to such a name in the procedure stays. The nested form (D234) and the opaque form (D233) are unchanged.
- **D237 — `try` is two commits, and its CFG half is #2230's** (VT10.4). The plan gives VT10.4 one change: every unhandled throw source of a `try` body reaches its `finally`, and a `TrySemantics` that answers `CompletionProtocol::Handlers`. Reading origin/rust first showed #2230 (3c2c2837) already fixing #2142 in the CFG builder, in thirty-one commits and about 840 lines of `cfg_lower.rs`, each commit a case review found: a nested `finally`, a `break` that passes through one, a process exit, a handler that catches only some completions, a `-` group, a handler that binds a variable. A smaller wiring here would be the first draft of that series, with its false W210s and its forwards of a value a `return` path never sets, and the merge would hold two implementations of each fact. So VT10.4 is VT10.4a, the registry's handler protocol (`HandlerChain`, `TrySemantics`, the `try` declaration), and VT10.4b, #2230's CFG change carried here with the handler facts read from the chain. The paragraph under VT10.4 names the facts and the files the merge settles. Two departures from the plan's text. Its program 1, `proc p {} {set f 0; try {error boom} finally {set f 1}; return $f}`, is not "neither W220 nor W210": the body always raises, so `return $f` never runs and both stores are dead, W220 is a true positive on each, and what the issue calls wrong is W210; the witness asserts W210 absent there and, for the variant that wraps the `try` in a `catch` so that the `return` runs, that the `finally` store is live and `set f 0` is the dead one. And the plan's "or `try_end` when there is none" is not carried: a `try` with no `finally` has no tail that its exits reach, since the exception resumes unwinding past it (#2230's doc says the same).
- **D238 — The handler list is read once, by the registry, and the plan states structure only** (VT10.4a). A `try`'s handlers are a list whose facts — which code each selects, which can never run, which scripts a match reaches — are asked by the CFG builder (the exception edges, the loop jumps, the exits `finally` is wired from), the executable IR's dispatch, and any later reader of the plan. #2230 answers them in four builder functions (`handler_code`, `handler_shadowed`, `live_handler_group`, `handler_misses_completion`) that compare the spellings `"on"` and `"trap"`; here the registry owns them. `HandlerChain` takes the handlers as links (`HandlerMatch`, the selector's text, whether the script is `-`) and the target's numerals, and answers `selected`, `code`, `owner`, `preempted`, `live_group`, `misses`, `takes` and `first_taking`. Three departures from #2230's text, each measured under tclsh 8.6, 9.0 and 9.1: pre-emption is judged against the handlers before a handler's group, not before the handler, so upstream's guard "never for the target of a `-` chain" (`earlier.last().is_some_and(|h| h.fallthrough)`), which its one call site cannot reach — `earlier` always ends in a handler that has a script — is not carried and the definition says what it did, that handlers of one group run one script and none pre-empts another; `first_taking` answers nothing when the first handler that might select the code is a `trap` or has a selector the registry cannot decode, where upstream's loop for a jump retargets an `on` only — the two agree for `break` and `continue`, which no `trap` selects, and the chain does not assume it; and the `ok` test of a handler group is the registry's decode (`takes(member, ok)`, so `on 0` is `on ok` under the target's numerals), as this branch's `push_try_handler_exception_edges` already had it, where upstream compares the spelling `ok`. The plan holds no selector text: a `HandlerPlan`'s `pattern` is an operand, and the chain is built from the links a consumer has — the IR's handlers for the CFG builder — so there is one decode and the plan needs no value. `TrySemantics` takes the command's clause grammar as a field, because `GRAMMAR` is private to its module, and the `try` spec declares it with its own, so the plan is read from the grammar the spec states and the clause shape is not written twice. The binders are positional — the first two elements of the variable list, an empty name kept as an empty `Declared` name — because the CFG's synthetic definition ignores which is which and a later reader of the result and options values needs to know; a third name is ignored, as `try` ignores it (`on error {a b c} {set a}` is `boom`).

- **D239 — #2230's CFG change is carried with the handler facts read from the chain** (VT10.4b). The functions D237's paragraph names are carried with upstream's names and bodies, adapted only where upstream reads the handler list: `handler_chain` builds the chain from the IR's handlers under the target's numerals (`Numbers::of_profile` of the registry's profile); the handler loop takes each owner's `live_group`, so a `-` handler and a fully pre-empted group get no edges; `push_try_handler_exception_edges` takes the group as chain indices and runs a group after normal completion alone when every member `takes` `ok`; `handler_misses_completion` is `HandlerChain::misses` over the block's exact code; `caught_by_handler` asks `takes` and looks for the edge into the `owner`'s block; `route_caught_loop_jumps` retargets a caught `break` or `continue` to the `owner` of `first_taking`; `try_handler_code` in the executable IR decodes through `HandlerChain::selected`. The region entries VT10.2 records stay in the branch that records them. The facts the CFG owns are carried as written: `try_ok` is normal completion (`try_completes_normally`), and a handler that binds a variable can raise before its exit (the binding statement makes the handler's block hold more than a lone `exit`).
- **D240 — O107 leaves a statement whose span holds code that runs** (VT10.4b). The carried change gives no edge to a handler an earlier one pre-empts, to a `-` handler and to one none of whose throw sources completes with a code it selects, and an `on ok` handler of a body that never completes is unreachable; the statement that binds a handler's variables carries the span of the whole `try`, so O107 deleted the `try` with the dead block. `proc p {} {try {error boom} on error {} {puts first} on 1 {m} {puts second}; puts after}; p` printed `after` once optimised where tclsh 8.6 to 9.1 print `first` and `after`, and `try {break} on error {m} {…}` in a loop lost its `break`. The binding's shape is the CFG's and the merge takes it as upstream wrote it, so the fix is the consumer's: `emit_unreachable` gathers the spans of what the reachable blocks run, statements and terminators, and leaves a dead statement whose span holds one; a dead handler loses its script and the `try` stays. A first fix in the builder, which dropped the binding from a handler block no edge enters, was reverted: it missed the `on ok` handler that SCCP alone proves dead (generated program `g1_0024`). `rust` (`ce7cf7f7`) has the same O107 and the same binding, so the defect is there too; reported.
- **D241 — A script leaves where its main path ends, and its dead code holds no throw point** (VT10.4b). `lower_script_inner` named the last block it lowered into as the script's terminal block, which is the orphan block of dead code when statements follow a `return`, `break` or `error`, and an `error` in that dead code was recorded as a throw point. A `try` body that cannot fall through is thrown to from its throw points, or from its terminal block when it has none, so `try {return r3; set v 8} on return {} {puts t8}` gave the handler an edge from dead code alone: the optimiser deleted `puts t8` and, where nothing else completes the `try`, the code after it (generated program `g1_0165`; `try {return r3; error dead}` the same through the dead throw point). The terminal block is now the one the main path ends in, and the throw points the dead code records are dropped. Pre-existing on HEAD and on `rust`, and fixed here because it is a `try` body's throw source, which VT10.4 is about; reported as well. Codegen builds read the terminal block only for whether a script falls through, which is unchanged, so the bytecode is as it was.

- **D242 — A `try` body is a protected region whose every statement, at any depth, ends a block a throw may leave from** (VT10.5; closes D225's open case). D223 split a flattened `catch` body per statement; a `try` body was one block per construct, so its handlers and `finally` were thrown to from the state before the body, its end and its explicit throws alone, and a store between two commands was dead to O109 and forwarded past by O102: `set x 1; try {set x 2; foo; set x 1} on error {} {}; puts $x` printed `1` once optimised, and `try {set x 2; foo; set x 3} finally {puts $x}` `3`, where tclsh 8.6 to 9.1 print `2`. In the analysis build the body is now a region (`SplitRegion::Try`) whose scripts split per statement — its own and those of every script it holds (an arm, a loop body, a handler or the `finally` of a nested `try`), save a nested `try` or `catch` body, which is a region of its own — and the exit of each block a split ends is a point (`SplitPoint`) for two reasons: a statement of the block may leave after its own stores, with any code, and the next statement may fail before it stores (`NextFailure`: an error alone from a literal assignment, which raises before it stores if it raises at all; nothing from a `catch` or a `try` with a `finally`, which runs a clause of its own first; any code otherwise). A point neither reason holds for is not one. Each live handler group takes the points by plain edges — a literal assignment's error only where a member may take an error, so `foreach i {1} {try {set y 1; set y 2; break} on break {} {puts $y}}` still forwards `puts 2` — and a nested `try` with no `finally` hands its body's points to the region around it (`escape_to_the_region_around`), since a completion none of its handlers takes leaves from where the body left.
